story.title: The First Boroughs
story.tagline: Two towns, one Capital City, and the name that whoever prospers gets to give.

sections.heading: Two towns and a Capital City
paragraphs: The First Boroughs are a town of animals, run by a Mayor, and the Mayor is you. There is a second Mayor with a second town, and between the two of them sits the Capital City, which belongs to neither and sells to both. Almost everything either town wants has to come across it.

A town holds ten animals at a time — at work, pledged into an auction, or face down in Unemployment — and that cap is the whole of the arithmetic. It is why a better animal is worth more than another animal, and why the question in front of a Mayor is never how many but which ten. Characters take work shifts to produce Supply, which is at once the town's money and its bidding power: the same coin pays a wage and wins a Building.

Work is organised by study — what an animal does. Agriculture, Civics, Commerce, Crafts, Lore and Science are the old six; Food was named when the café by the Hiring Hall became the place half the borough's business got done, and Entertainment was the last the borough admitted it had, which is why its token was struck last of the eight. Species is what an animal is, and there are ten of them, each with a charter of its own. Both are settled facts here. An animal can change what it does. It does not change what it is.

sections.heading: The Capital City is the market, and the Capital City is the judge
paragraphs: The Capital City is the shared market. Buildings, hired animals, Ordinances and the nine Statues are all won there, in bidding wars, by whichever Mayor puts up the Supply. A Building is the Capital City's and is taken at auction; what the borough then does with it is the borough's own business, which is how a Physic Garden built to grow specimens came to be full of animals instead.

The room has its own weather. The Auction House has a horseshoe nailed over the door the wrong way up and half the borough says that lets the luck out. The steward has views about calling out over a lot and has had them since before either Mayor was in office. The Sealed Bid puts one figure in writing in a box, which Faustus loathes because there is nothing in it for anybody to watch — and Faustus, who dresses the bidders, is not wrong that a well-cut coat has already cost everybody a rung before a number is said. Barrow walks a lot before the auction and comes back with a figure the Capital City has never once beaten by more than a Supply, and Orien, fed shift returns and auction prices, will tell you what a Building will go for and be right.

The Ordinances are the Capital City's mood written down: a Monument Tax on a borough rich enough to raise a monument, a Masons' Rate when the quarry has more stone cut than orders for it, a Timber Levy the week the price of a roof goes up, a Building Grant worded so plainly the Counting House read it four times looking for the catch. And the Capital City comes out to you as well — the Tax Assessors arrive with clipboards and nobody remembers inviting them, and both Mayors are called in to a conference on the same short notice and both come home having hired somebody on the spot.

sections.heading: Incorporation, and what the fifth Statue actually buys
paragraphs: Holding five Statues wins the game, and each of the nine grants a boon and imposes a burden, so a Mayor who collects them is also collecting the things they cost. But a majority of the Statues is not a trophy. It is the Capital City's own test of which borough is the prosperous one, and the Capital City settles the result the way it has always settled it: the prosperous town incorporates the other.

Nothing is razed and nobody is turned out. The wards are merged, the two Hiring Halls put up one board, and every animal in both towns keeps their work. What closes is the charter. The incorporated town's Mayor is no longer a Mayor, and the single town that results takes whatever name the winning Mayor gives it. That is what the fifth Statue actually buys — not the town next door, but the right to say what all of it is called from then on.

This has happened before. It is why the place is called the First Boroughs and not the First Borough, and why the older names survive only on Ned's shelves: three closed charters, under names nobody here uses out loud, two of them printed by Scott and certified by Ned. The borough does not remember being incorporated as a defeat and does not remember it as a kindness either. It remembers it as the year the board changed and the work carried on, and any animal old enough may have been on the wrong side of one.

sections.heading: The year the bridge went
paragraphs: The borough dates things by two bad seasons. One is the winter the Grain Exchange shut for six weeks. The other is the spring the bridge went, and because Scott will not print a year Ned has not certified, when Scott says which spring it was the borough stops arguing about it.

What the bridge did was take the short way out of town. Adam was on the county road for most of that spring keeping the carts moving the long way round, which cost a day on every load and which he has never once claimed as anything. Copper did not open the cellar under the weights office — he lent the salt out on the quiet and said there would be worse, exactly as he did the winter the Exchange shut. Quinn was at the back of the bad meeting afterwards with the book open. Robbie headlined the inquiry A SPAN OF ATTENTION and laughed at it alone in the office for some time.

It is still the borough's measuring stick. Beck reads ward minutes nobody has wanted since the bridge went; Lynnette carries the water-stained novels from the same shelf out to the bonfire every year; FutureTech posted a record quarter in that year as it does in every year. The Boroughs are not sentimental about it. They mention the bridge the way other towns mention a date.

sections.heading: Coming out, and going back
paragraphs: The Capital City is a real place, and animals emigrate from it. Barrow cut stone there for twenty years — frontages, stairs, work admired by animals who would never know his name — and came out to the First Boroughs precisely because the First Boroughs are not finished being built. He wanted a wall he set this spring to still be the wall everyone walks past in thirty years.

Brett is the other half of that story: the same city, the opposite decision. He practises in the Capital City, comes out when the borough needs somebody who knows exactly how the Capital City's rules are written, wins it, bills for it, and takes the evening coach home. The Counting House budgets for him a year ahead.

Most of what comes out is hired rather than settled. Kevin arrived at seventeen because somebody said there was work: eleven jobs by nineteen, worth two of anybody for a fortnight, and every one of those eleven would have him back. Jake came out with a reputation the Hiring Hall has never been given the details of, runs the warrens' long errands, takes the money in his paw rather than on the book, and is gone before anybody has decided anything about him. Cornelius runs FutureTech and is retained rather than recruited, and he does not stay either. Tuppence comes out about once a month with a cart. Eustace comes out for a season, the way Capital City socialites do, and the whole town runs a little faster for exactly as long as he is here.

It goes the other way too, in smaller ways. Yellow came up from the suburbs at the edge of the Capital City and built a whole catalogue out of what the borough actually has. Eric's parents are Capital City lawyers who took a six-year-old at his word about farming and then learned it alongside him. Velvet came out as a petition runner at seventeen and has been behind one counter or another ever since.

sections.heading: FutureTech, and the Capital City's newer lots
paragraphs: FutureTech is the Capital City's technology company and the newest thing in the town's record. FutureTech HQ is glass to the fourth floor, with a lobby anyone may walk through and two floors nobody may. The borough's own FutureTech Store sells what came off those floors a month ago. Starfish Coffee, the land's coffee chain, is FutureTech's and is run by automatons. The Hospital has been theirs since the spring, repainted, with every one of its staff kept on. The company posts a record quarter every quarter. Nobody has been past the second floor, and nobody can say where the automatons go when a job is finished — Robbie has asked Cornelius in print four times and come away each time having learned a great deal about something else.

It reaches into the borough more quietly than that. FutureTech funds a Science Lab here, a bench and a bay kept separate from the Hospital's books and the Store's till, where the borough's own Science animals work free of the Capital City's usual terms. Cynthia's desk is in it, and the Science hall has stopped asking where the money comes from.

The Capital City's newer lots are the other half of the same reach: the Bookstore, the Game Store, the Juice Store, the Gas Station, the Cheese Store, the Bank, the Fast Food Joint, the Car Dealership, the Owlery and the Airport. The borough has a forecourt, a filling station and an airfield, and has had all three for longer than anybody bothers to say. The Capital City put them up; what the borough does with them is its own business, exactly as it is with the Physic Garden.

sections.heading: The working day, and the night
paragraphs: A working day here is a shift, and a shift pays Supply. The board goes up at the Hiring Hall, Henrietta gossips about all of it from the front desk, Nancy fills the fast small jobs off the temp board a few feet along the same counter, and a lean season is not a disaster — it is a season with nothing on, a bare board by Tuesday, and Quinn turning back four years for the animals who did that exact work in the last one.

The night is not an afterthought in this town; it is a second town. There is an observatory, an all-night café, a night school and Owls who work while the rest of the borough sleeps. Hoot keeps the ward's keys and a standing list of animals who have asked to be woken, and knocks at four in the morning on anybody who is on it — being woken here is a service you sign up for, not something that happens to you. The night round's lamps are filled at Benjamin's bench and nowhere else, which is his rule and not the ward's, and Mandee carries them.

Everything else follows the same hours. Marmalade bakes at night because that is when the ovens are banked, and hands it out in the morning to the kittens first. Hazel's trestles go up when the lamps go on and come down around four. Taco's cart is shut at noon and open at four in the morning for the lightermen. Barnaby audits the night's books and is gone before the first shift bell. Andrew keeps the Lending Library's late desk after the children's corner has emptied. Jessica's night school starts at ten and has no homework, and half the Hiring Hall's promotions these ten years started in that room. By the time the rest of the borough is up, the night has quietly put half of tomorrow in order.

sections.heading: What the two towns do together
paragraphs: For two towns competing for a Capital City's monuments, the First Boroughs spend a remarkable amount of time in each other's company. Shay does her rounds twice and the second round crosses the ward boundary, on the grounds that an animal asleep on their feet is an animal asleep on their feet whichever Mayor's town they are standing in. It has been raised at three meetings and has never once been stopped. Oatmeal's benefit night hands over whatever the hall takes without checking which town it is going to, and his awning down the length of the square gets the rival Mayor's animal under it too, which the ward office regards as a filing problem.

The fixtures are shared on purpose. The Community Bonfire burns the year's broken pallets on the far field one night a year, and the other town walks over the hill for it and is handed a chair. The Car Show is held on market day and nobody has ever moved it, because the square is already full and both boroughs turn out. The Casino Fundraiser puts table games in the Long Hall for one night, run by whoever the Capital City sends out, and the till comes out roughly even by morning whatever went in. The Friendship Festival pairs up Cats and Mice for the day on the grounds that neither species is naturally the other's friend, and the borough has been quietly pleased for years at how often it works.

And a good deal of it is nobody's plan at all. Half the other town is in the queue at the Ice Cream Shop on a warm afternoon and none of them are at work. Whatever the other town arrives holding, some of it goes in the Gas Station's bin before they leave. The babies of both boroughs will sit in front of the Clinic's coral tank for an hour. When somebody with a chart says a comet is passing, the whole square goes out on its back on the cobbles, and half the borough's best trades have been agreed lying there, because nobody haggles well looking up.

sections.heading: The residents, at a glance
paragraphs: Ten species live here — Rabbits, Mice, Badgers, Hedgehogs, Raccoons, Foxes, Otters, Squirrels, Cats and Owls — and each has a charter of its own and a way of working that goes with it. Badgers start slowly and then do not stop. Squirrels are poor all year and rich exactly once. Cats do as they please. Otters do nothing slowly, and an Otter Pup is the only slow thing an Otter will ever be. Owls keep the hours nobody else wants and get paid for it fourteen years later.

The eight studies cut across all of that. An animal in this borough is a Commerce animal or a Crafts animal or a Food animal before it is anything else at work, and a good many of them hold two or three — the same animal keeps the weights and buys at the bottom of the day, or nurses the children's ward and runs the restaurant's juice list three evenings a week.

Two smaller groups belong to the town as much as anybody. There are eighteen figures nobody could name: when a post here is worked by an animal who gives no name, Ned will not leave the entry blank and will not invent a name for it, so the record says what the ward saw — the masked otter, the hooded rabbit, the clerk at the second window. Almost always some animal the borough already knows turns out to have been the one standing there, and Ned files the correction as a correction and not a promotion. And there are the babies, one for every species, put on light work early with the post kept open behind them: a Bunny on a row, a Hoglet on the gate step, a Badger Cub in the corner of the workshop with a block nobody explains. Three days of any of them is about one animal's morning, and the ward counts a Baby Mouse, a Badger Cub, a Raccoon Kit, a Fox Cub and an Owlet at two, because their first season is held to be half the trade.

capital.name: Capital City
capital.tagline: The shared market between two Mayors' towns, and the judge of which of them is prospering. Buildings, hired animals, Ordinances and the nine Statues are all won here.

history.heading: What the Capital City is
paragraphs: The Capital City sits between two Mayors' towns and belongs to neither. It is the shared market: Buildings, hired animals, Ordinances and the nine Statues are won there in bidding wars, and Supply earned on a shift in either borough is spent in the same room.

It is also bigger, faster and older than either of its neighbours, and it knows it. It has its own professional class, which the borough buys by the day. It runs a fee schedule for everything, printed, which Copper has read all of and knows which parts of can be got round. It keeps a steward who will need a long afternoon and somebody to have it with before he will call out over a lot.

history.heading: How it treats the boroughs
paragraphs: A Building is the Capital City's and is won at auction; the borough's use of it is its own business. That single rule explains most of what the two places are to each other. The borough has bought the Weighbridge at the Grain Exchange, the Counting House, the Town Workshop, the Guild Hall, the Long Room, the All-Night Café, the Hiring Hall, the Festival Green, the Winter Stores and the Physic Garden out of the Capital City, and has then done with them whatever it wanted — which is how a garden built to grow specimens came to be full of animals.

The traffic the other way is less welcome and just as regular. The Tax Assessors come out with clipboards, unannounced, and the borough loses Supply when they do; Copper has met them four times and has never once been surprised. The Capital City would like it minuted that a borough rich enough to raise a monument is a borough rich enough to be asked about it. When it stops signing, the first names off any board are the ones who have been on it the shortest.

It also calls. Both Mayors are summoned to a conference on short and identical notice and both come home having hired somebody on the spot, with no time yet to put the new hire properly to work. And some seasons it sends a Casino Fundraiser out to the Long Hall for a night, open to both boroughs, run by whoever it happens to send, with the till coming out roughly even by morning whatever went in.

history.heading: The Statues, and the quarry that holds the rest
paragraphs: The Statues are the town's stated virtues, cut out of one quarry over a great many years. Nine stand in the Capital City in any one year and the rest are still in the quarry, which is why two animals can honestly remember a different set, and why which nine monuments pass through the Capital City is not the same from one year to the next.

The quarry is a working concern with a working concern's problems. Some seasons it has more stone cut than it has orders for, and Barrow has costed the difference on the back of a docket and posted it where both Mayors will walk past it. Some seasons nothing carved comes down the road at all, because the long pull to the county gate went in the wet and nothing moves until it is made. And some seasons the Capital City discovers it has nowhere to put a monument, because Adam has the square up for the cobbles and will not be hurried about it.

history.heading: FutureTech
paragraphs: FutureTech is the Capital City's technology company and the newest thing in the town's record. Its HQ is glass to the fourth floor, with a lobby anyone may walk through and two floors nobody may. Starfish Coffee, the land's coffee chain, is FutureTech's and is run by automatons. The Hospital has been theirs since the spring, repainted, with every one of its staff kept on. The borough's own FutureTech Store sells what came off those floors a month ago.

Cornelius runs it, is retained by the Capital City whenever the books will not balance, and arrives with three automatons and a folder. The costings are right, the buildings do go up cheaper, and the ward comes away with a schedule that works and a faint sense of having agreed to something it cannot now find in writing. A machine on the site on Friday is not on the site on Monday and is not in the yard, the store or the scrap, and nobody can say where it went. The company posts a record quarter every quarter, including the year the bridge went.

history.heading: The newer lots
paragraphs: The Bookstore, the Game Store, the Juice Store, the Gas Station, the Cheese Store, the Bank, the Fast Food Joint, the Car Dealership, the Owlery and the Airport are the Capital City's newest building work. The borough has a forecourt, a filling station and an airfield and has had all three for longer than anybody bothers to say; the Capital City put these up, and the borough's use of them is its own business in the usual way.

They are not received identically. The Owlery was built as a post house and the Owls moved in the first winter, which has made the post a side effect ever since. The Bank does not care what kind of chit you bring it, which no other counter in the First Boroughs can say. Marmalade has never said a word against the Fast Food Joint, which from Marmalade is the loudest thing anybody has said about it. And the Grocery Store, which is older than any of them and owned by nobody in particular, goes on selling bread and milk to a queue that has never once discussed the Capital City.

history.heading: Animals hired out of the city
paragraphs: Animals are bought out of the Capital City the same way Buildings are, and they behave differently for it. Brett practises there and comes out by the day. Cornelius is retained rather than recruited. Kevin came out at seventeen looking for work and has had eleven jobs by nineteen. Jake came out with a reputation nobody has been given the details of and leaves before anyone has decided anything about him. Tuppence brings a cart out about once a month with things nobody here yet has a use for. Eustace comes out for a season and leaves as suddenly as he arrived.

Barrow is the exception that makes the pattern legible: twenty years cutting stone in the Capital City, and then out to the Boroughs for good, specifically because the Boroughs are not finished being built. The rest come out, do the work better than anybody available, and go back.

places.name: The Festival Green
places.summary: The Capital City's open ground, and the reason Entertainment is a study.
paragraphs: It was here before this Mayor and it will be here after, and on any given evening there is a band on it that nobody booked. Entertainment became a study because of what kept happening here after the shift ended.

The Bandstand on it was built for speeches and has never once been used for one; it holds a band of five if two of them stand on the step. Daisy's garlands go up for festival week, four days and a year's takings in one go. Tabitha turned up with a borrowed camera and stayed long after everyone else's memory of the day had gone soft, which is how the borough started asking her for prints. Liza has turned the Green down twice on the grounds that it is too big a room to be honest in. Fred was near the Bandstand during a speech nobody has ever actually given from it, and says he was looking for the toilets.

In daylight it is where the hiring gets done outdoors: the Apprentice Fair on the first fine Saturday in March, where Berry has never once come away without somebody, and the trestle tables of an open hiring fair with a queue that moves surprisingly fast, because half of it has already spent a season on Rosabeth's beds.

places.name: The Apprentice School
places.summary: One of the Capital City's Buildings, and not where most of the borough's apprentices actually learn.
paragraphs: The Apprentice School stands in the Capital City with the Festival Green and the Long Hall, and a Mayor who wins it wins a Building like any other. What the borough has noticed is how little of its own apprenticing goes through it.

The apprentice notices in the Hiring Hall are Lynnette's, set and printed and pinned up free, which is why an animal here can find out how to be better at their job without knowing anybody first. The rest of it happens on a bench or over a counter: Berry putting the thing in your paws and asking what you think is wrong with it, Moss taking the apprentice nobody else wants, Earl talking half the borough's apprentices into the next thing over a pot they did not pay for, and Jessica's night school at ten at night, where half the Hiring Hall's promotions these ten years started.

places.name: The Observatory
places.summary: The dome, the selection board, and the bench where the lenses are ground.
paragraphs: The Observatory and the Science hall run a selection board for who goes up, and it turns animals down. It turned Comet down twice before she got the seat on her third application; Winter sat it twice and came away with two courteous letters and no seat, and ended up reading the manifests and the order book for a different room entirely. Sage has had the application form left on their desk three times and put it back in the drawer three times, and knows the space division better than it knows itself.

The instruments are Sota's. Every small one came off their bench and the two big ones have been re-seated twice, months of work with the last of it done by hand, and Sota has no interest whatever in what any of them are pointed at. Tabitha spent two winters at that bench arguing about focal length. Tuppence once brought a crate of ribbed glass out on the cart that the Observatory later turned out to want very badly, and Orien's calculating engine is built half out of what the Observatory threw away.

Other animals are on it without being of it. Inkwell is on the steps with a flask most nights. Juniper keeps the telescope hire book. Mittens has been seen on the dome on a clear night, and so has Fingers, coming down off it. Cynthia keeps a bench at the back of the Science hall that the Observatory has quietly stopped asking her to tidy. And there is an observation book from the months the big instrument was a blank, in a hand the Observatory does not have on file and has never had cause to doubt.

places.name: The Grain Exchange
places.summary: The borough's biggest building, and one of its two reference points for a bad season.
paragraphs: Everything the borough grows and everything it sells on passes through the Grain Exchange, and the borough's memory of it is mostly the winter it shut for six weeks. Copper did not open his cellar that winter either; he lent the salt out on the quiet, said there would be worse, and every animal who was put back to work that February was put back by a neighbour.

Its returns are patchy in the Exchange's own hands and complete in somebody else's: Annabelle pulled a year of them out of the Salvage Yard before the weather got at it, and that year exists nowhere else, because the Exchange threw its own copy out. Finn had a weighing job here and lost it, which the borough mentions to neither him nor to Liz, who has the plate now.

places.name: The Weighbridge
places.summary: Liz's plate at the Grain Exchange, which every loaded cart in or out of the borough crosses.
paragraphs: Every loaded cart in or out of the borough crosses Liz's plate and is paid on what she writes. Copper's office certifies the bridge each spring and has never once had to adjust it, which Copper mentions every spring and Liz has never once looked up for.

Liz is a Fox and reads a carter's face while the beam is settling, and has never needed to do anything about what she reads there, because the beam settles where it settles. The weight of every cart she has ever put on the plate goes into Orien's engine along with the shift returns and the ferry's crossings, which is how the almanac's price tables come out. There is also a second hand that has turned up beside the night figures about twice a year for years, agreeing to the last halfpenny, whose scale figures Liz says have never once needed adjusting.

places.name: The Hiring Hall
places.summary: The board, the two desks, and half the borough's second chances.
paragraphs: Half its second chances were somebody else's first. An animal who has stopped getting up is sent to Rosabeth's gate, spends a season on the beds and comes back through this door, and Biff has walked more animals up these steps than anyone has counted. Quinn turns back four years when a place falls vacant and hands over a slip with a name on it, and more animals have been got back into work by that slip than by any committee sitting.

It runs two desks a Rabbit and a Raccoon have made their own. Henrietta's front desk posts the board and gossips about all of it, invented characters included, and is the best-informed and least reliable animal in either borough; Nancy's temp board a few feet along the same counter is shorter, louder and how the borough's fast, small jobs get filled inside a day. The back room holds an old friends' reunion once a year that nobody has ever called a reunion to its face.

It is also the borough's filing cabinet for the things it cannot explain. There is no address on file for Barnaby, none for Mandee, none for Jake, and the line for Mittens says Mittens and nothing else. The standing complaints about the late mail cart, the fish and the late second post are all here and none of them has ever come to anything. On a lean week the board is bare by Tuesday; on a short week there are four days on it instead of six, posted without comment, and Gwen's counter is busy by nine and Bean's by ten.

places.name: The Salvage Yard
places.summary: Divided three ways without anybody having said so.
paragraphs: Everything the borough throws out comes here, and the yard has divided itself without a word being spoken about it. Annabelle takes the paper, pulling it out before the weather gets at it: ward minutes, split almanacs, bills of lading, half a novel, a year of the Grain Exchange's returns that exists nowhere else. Patch takes everything else, mends what is worth mending and sells it back to the borough at a price nobody has ever complained about — although what Patch is really known for is the judging, which started with carts and now covers leases and seasons that have not gone well, and he is right. Gabe takes the third pile, which is what Patch has looked at and put down, and makes puppets out of it.

Patch's counter is a plank across two barrels and the verdict comes over it in about four seconds. What he will not take, Pockets will, and does not say whose it was. There is a shelf at knee height that nobody stocks and that is never empty, carried in one piece at a time from the City Dump by Raccoon Kits too small to carry two, and Pockets prices it exactly as seriously as anything else in the yard and got the ward to count the post at two on that argument. Fingers has mended locks here between one season's work and the next.

places.name: The Long Hall
places.summary: One of the Capital City's Buildings, and where the Casino Fundraiser is held.
paragraphs: The Long Hall stands in the Capital City's own list of Buildings, alongside the Festival Green and the Old Wall. What both boroughs know it for is the Casino Fundraiser: table games in the Long Hall for one night, open to both towns, run by whoever the Capital City sends out. The till comes out roughly even between the two towns by morning whatever went in the night before.

places.name: The Old Wall
places.summary: One of the Capital City's Buildings, and not the sort of wall the borough builds for itself.
paragraphs: The Old Wall is a Capital City Building and comes up for auction like any other. The borough's own walls are a different proposition and are raised by its own animals. The Quill Wall is not much of a wall — Bob leans on it, Biff walks past it four times a night, Berry has mended the gate in it twice without being asked — and nothing has ever got over it. The Ironwood Palisade is twice-mended and ivy to the top and charmingly unimpressive until you try to get over it, with Quill asleep on the inside of it.

places.name: The Counting House
places.summary: The borough's money, Mildred's counter, and the figures Orien's engine produces.
paragraphs: The Counting House budgets for Brett a year ahead and has stopped querying Tuppence's prices, and both of those are Orien's doing: he feeds the shift returns, the auction prices, the ferry's crossings and the weight of every cart Liz has put on her plate into an engine built out of Observatory cast-offs, and the figure comes back within a Supply. Lynnette sets the tables he supplies and nobody in the borough has paid for a figure since.

Mildred has been behind the counter for forty-one years and has never made an error; Ned has checked, twice, unasked. She is friendly and absolutely immovable about the rules, and she says no to a Mayor exactly as she says it to anybody else, which is the single most expensive habit in the First Boroughs and the reason the borough's money has never once gone missing. What a Mayor across the table notices is subtler: while Mildred is on her feet there is simply a form, and the form is correct, and the form takes a while.

The borough keeps its own long desk of the same name, two lamps and the quarterly returns in order of age, where Copper weighs what comes in and Peanut works out what it was worth, usually between orders and usually before being asked. The Founder's Grant is voted here and paid in one lump, and the chit is the part that lasts. A Building Grant worded plainly enough gets read four times looking for the catch.

places.name: The Auction House
places.summary: Where the lots go, and where a coat is worth a rung before a number is said.
paragraphs: There is a horseshoe nailed over the door the wrong way up, which half the borough says lets the luck out and the other half says pours it on whoever is standing underneath. Inside it, the borough's outfits are Faustus's: he will not make a thing for a room he is not going to be in, and a Mayor who turns up to the Capital City in something he made has cost everybody else a rung before a number has been said. The Auction House has stopped pretending otherwise.

Not everything is decided in the room. The Sealed Bid puts one figure in writing in a box to be opened at the hour, which Faustus loathes because there is nothing in it for anybody to watch. A good deal of it is settled beforehand over the second pot at Earl's. Robbie is unusually good at knowing what is coming into the Capital City before it is put up and saying so in print, which is a kind of power the auction house has never worked out how to take off him, and Eustace is owed favours by half the Capital City's auction houses.

Fox Cubs are not allowed inside and every one of them knows what the big lots went for. They sit on the steps and read the faces of the animals coming out, and a Fox Cub who has read the faces wrong twice does not read them wrong a third time. Nothing in the Auction House is taught; it is watched from the steps until it is obvious, which is why the ward counts the steps at two and the Auction House has never once objected.

places.name: The Winter Stores
places.summary: The town's stores, stocked off Copper's list and baked for by Cookie.
paragraphs: Copper drew up the list the borough works from — salt, lamp oil, candle stock — and then built the one thing his own cellar has never had: a door somebody else is allowed to open. He says the town's stores are for the town, and his are for later.

Cookie bakes for them. Everything off her board is made to keep and to be opened in a different season from the one it was made in: hard biscuit, twice-baked rusk, seed cake that improves for a month and is edible for a year. She works the late heat of the Community Oven after the bread is out, which is the cool slow end nobody else wants and exactly the end she needs, and she dates the shelf in pencil and has never once been wrong about how long it would have to last.

places.name: The Lending Library
places.summary: The children's corner, the late desk, and the low shelf that made an astronomer.
paragraphs: The children's corner has two regular readers: Inkwell tells the little ones about the worlds on the other side of ours one evening a week, and Lynnette reads on Thursdays, on the floor, doing all the voices. The lanterns are Benjamin's, filled at his bench like every other lamp in the borough and hung low enough for a mouse to read by. Gabe's puppet show has the Saturday-morning slot the two of them do not use. A young animal in this borough has been read to by one or both.

The shelves have made careers. Sage learned to read on the low shelf, which is where the scientific romances live, and read the lot before they were ten. Comet read every book the Library had before she wrote to the Observatory. There is a photograph here of Clover in a rocket holding a tray of seed potatoes and looking extremely pleased. The lower shelves were reorganised by somebody at Baby Mouse height, which nobody asked for and which is, annoyingly, better.

Andrew keeps the late desk after the children's corner has emptied and the evening readers have gone, copying by hand what cannot be lent out, a page or two a night, so that there is a second one; the Library has twice filed his copy as the original. Twice now he has come in to find the night's pages already done in a hand that is not his and is better than his. Above it all is the Spare Room, which whoever has it has until they do not need it, and three of the names on the ward book got their start in it.

places.name: The Long Room
places.summary: The Lending Library's upper floor, where the ribbons live.
paragraphs: The Lending Library's upper floor, where the ribbons live and the reading lamps are never all out. Inkwell has a chair in it that everybody knows is theirs and nobody has ever said so out loud, and Inkwell's star chart was made entirely from that chair, which means half the sky is missing and the half that is there is right to the minute.
The Lore tokens are kept in the long drawer with the ribbons. Lynnette prints the replacements, and the replacements are better than the originals, which Inkwell finds very funny.

places.name: The Town Workshop
places.summary: The jigs, the loan book, and the room Berry answers to when the clock stops.
paragraphs: It keeps the jigs, the loan book and the standing argument about whether Moss's bench jig counts as the Workshop's now that half the borough uses it. Berry answers to this room when the Town Clock stops and has never once been asked to explain anything else. The Workshop has stopped sending anybody to check on Moss, who reads the sheet, puts it down, and does the thing that works, and lets the result argue.

Balto's shop is off the Town Workshop court, and any bench, chair or shelf in the borough with a neat dovetail joint and no record of ever being commissioned probably came off it. A Badger Cub is put in a corner of the workshop with a block and a blunt gouge and is not spoken to for a fortnight, which is not neglect but the whole of the Badger method, and every Badger in the First Boroughs has been through it.

places.name: The Guild Hall
places.summary: The engine course, the intake list, and the committee that offers two things.
paragraphs: The engine course runs here twice a year and the intake list goes up on the door the week before. Comet took it twice because she did not think she had understood it the first time; she had, and she wanted to be sure. Barrow will not join and turns up anyway, on the grounds that somebody has to tell them about foundations.

Hazel has run the guild hall twice and sits on the market committee, which sits over the guildhall, has a cat for a weathervane that nobody will admit to paying for, and learned long ago to put two proposals it can live with in front of a room rather than one it cannot. Hazel arrives at both in the coat they closed the stall in. Lynnette gives the guild its syllabus free. Moss's formal warning from the Capital City is the guild's other kind of paperwork, and it came across Velvet's counter.
Guild Night clears the bench and brings out the good chairs, and whatever anyone is stuck on goes round the table once; Berry says nothing for an hour and then says the thing that fixes it.

places.name: The Physic Garden
places.summary: Built to grow specimens; used to grow animals.
paragraphs: The Capital City built it to grow specimens and the borough uses it to grow animals. Rosabeth runs it: whoever is out of work that month is on the beds by the end of the week, and is not told that they are being mended. She will not be drawn on the tinctures — the Science hall has twice failed to account for them and has stopped writing it up — but she is perfectly clear about the rest of it. You are not here to be mended; you are here because the beds want doing.

Shay keeps her surgery two doors away, and Rosabeth's garden and the Science hall are on speaking terms because of her and not before her. The queue at an open hiring fair moves surprisingly fast because half of it has already spent a season on these beds and is fit to be somewhere else.

places.name: The All-Night Café
places.summary: Bean's, by the Hiring Hall, open when everything else is shut.
paragraphs: Bean's, by the Hiring Hall, open when everything else is shut. Peanut keeps its books and works the day counter; Bean owns it and has never once been seen sitting down. They open before the early shift and are still wiping down when the night workers come off.

It is the night's own counter. On the night round Bean opens up, Hoot does the doors and Barnaby is already at the ledger, and by the time the rest of the borough is up the night has quietly put half of tomorrow in order. There is an Otter Pup under the counter most nights and Bean has never once asked whose; they come in off the ferry steps with the lightermen, are handed something warm and are put to work carrying it two tables over, which takes an extremely long time and involves the entire room. The café's Food tokens live in the till under the tray and Peanut counts them with the takings every night whether or not anybody has asked.

places.name: The Owlery
places.summary: Built as a post house; occupied by Owls since the first winter.
paragraphs: Brick, tall, and warm at the top, and the Capital City built it as a post house. The Owls moved in the first winter and the post has been a side effect ever since. There has to be one of them up there already or the rest do not come: Hoot keeps the list, and Hoot has never had to look at it.
The Owl tokens are collected at dusk rather than at the Hiring Hall's hours, after Hoot pointed out mildly that every Owl in the borough was asleep at eleven in the morning.

places.name: The Bank
places.summary: The only counter in the First Boroughs that does not care what kind of chit you brought it.
paragraphs: Mildred's counter, and the only place in the First Boroughs that does not care what kind of chit you have brought it. Two is two. She will count them in front of you, slowly, and she will be right.

It is a newer lot and it behaves like an older one, which is Mildred's doing: forty-one years without an error, the rule explained, the reason for the rule explained, and then no, today, to a Mayor in the same words as to anybody else.

places.name: The Fast Food Joint
places.summary: Open at all hours, out in under a minute, and nobody has worked a full season in it.
paragraphs: Open at all hours, out in under a minute, and the whole town suddenly has time it did not have. Nobody has worked a full season in it and nobody can say in advance whose last week it is.
Marmalade has never said a word against the place, which from Marmalade is the loudest thing anybody has said about it.

places.name: The Car Dealership
places.summary: Bunting, a brass bell and a Fox on the forecourt.
paragraphs: Bunting, a brass bell and a Fox on the forecourt. Nobody has ever walked off this lot poorer and emptier-pawed at the same time, which is the whole art of it: you are four Supply down and you are driving something home and you cannot decide how you feel.

The Car Show is held on market day and nobody has ever moved it. The Fox on the forecourt opens it, the ledger animals make it add up, and both boroughs turn out — which is exactly why it is held on the day the square is already full.

places.name: The Airport
places.summary: One strip and a windsock, and a day is a day.
paragraphs: Reese's field, one strip and a windsock, and Mimi runs the whole of the rest of it. An animal off the morning aircraft is standing in your town by nine and gone by supper, and the borough has decided that a day is a day.

Reese holds the borough's only instrument ticket and is the one who goes when the weather has shut the ferry. Mimi works the cabin, which is five jobs in a uniform designed to look like one, and moves between all five so smoothly that most passengers come off believing they have been looked after by one extremely calm rabbit and not by a small institution.

places.name: FutureTech HQ
places.summary: Glass to the fourth floor, a lobby anyone may walk through and two floors nobody may.
paragraphs: Glass to the fourth floor, a lobby you may walk through and two floors you may not, and a company that posts a record quarter in a year the bridge went. Cornelius will show you everything. He will show you the second floor last, and then the tour will be over.

Nobody has been past the second floor and nobody can say where the automatons go when a job is finished. A machine that was on the site on Friday is not on the site on Monday and is not in the yard, the store or the scrap. Robbie has asked in print four times and been answered warmly, at length, and with figures, about something else.

places.name: The FutureTech Store
places.summary: The borough's branch, selling what came off those floors a month ago.
paragraphs: Everything in the window is a month old and everything behind the counter is a fortnight. Jim is in the queue on launch day whatever it is, and the whole street is richer for the queue.

On Release Day the line starts at the store, goes past the coffee bar, which is FutureTech's too, and round to the HQ steps, which are FutureTech's as well. Jim is second. Jim is always second, and has never once explained who is first. He has bought everything, including the automated candle, which is why there is a patch on the left side of his head where the fur came back a different colour.

places.name: Starfish Coffee
places.summary: The land's coffee chain, FutureTech's, and not an animal behind the counter.
paragraphs: The land's coffee chain, the borough's branch, and not an animal behind the counter: three automatons, a menu board that changes itself, and a FutureTech name on the receipt in very small print. The queue moves faster than anywhere else in town.

It is the only counter in the borough that nobody has to be got back on their feet at. Bean's has the mornings and the accounts and the noise, and Earl's has the long afternoons, and neither of them has ever competed with the other for an hour.

places.name: The Hospital
places.summary: FutureTech's since the spring, repainted, with every one of its staff kept on.
paragraphs: Pristine, quiet, and owned since the spring by FutureTech, which repainted the wards and kept every one of the staff. An animal who stops getting up goes in through those doors and comes out fit for a shift, which is more than the borough could say a year ago.

Shay is the borough's doctor and reads the three medical journals that come up on the late ferry the night they arrive. JT took the children's ward — nobody assigned it — and has a bit for every procedure in it, most of them terrible, all of them load-bearing, because an animal who is laughing is an animal who is not bracing. The Science Lab FutureTech funds in the borough is kept a floor below the Hospital's books.

places.name: The Bookstore
places.summary: Ned's overflow, priced by somebody else and sold by nobody in particular.
paragraphs: Ned's overflow, priced by somebody else and sold by nobody in particular. You never leave with nothing and you never leave with room in the bag, which is why the shelf by the door is for what you have decided against on the way out.

Beck does not shop here; he takes in what the borough throws out and prefers the ones nobody else wanted. Kevin does, in a manner of speaking — Lynnette keeps him a shelf at the print shop instead and has never charged him for a novel.

places.name: The Game Store
places.summary: Dice, boards, and painted figures that are not Dirt's.
paragraphs: Dice, boards, painted figures an inch and a half tall that are not Dirt's and are sold as though they were. Supply goes in over the counter and comes back out as something to do on a Tuesday, which the borough has decided is a fair rate.

Dirt carves and paints the borough's cast out of hours, one at a time, a season each. Ned has eleven of them on the ward-record shelf, one of which is labelled DIRT and is unmistakably Squirt, and has not been corrected in four years.

places.name: The Juice Store
places.summary: JT drew up the list and then went back to the restaurant.
paragraphs: JT drew up the list and then went back to the restaurant, and the counter has been run ever since by whoever is nearest. Somebody is always back behind it. It is not always somebody who meant to be.

The restaurant's juice list is the serious version and is taken seriously: JT runs it three evenings a week in a clean shirt, it pairs the Auction House's big lots, and a child at the next table is never served anything less interesting than what the adults are drinking.

places.name: The Cheese Store
places.summary: A cold room, a marble slab and a queue of two species.
paragraphs: A cold room, a marble slab and a queue of two species. The Mice buy it. The Raccoons are here for the rind bin round the back, which the shop has stopped pretending is not the main trade.

The cellar under the shop is Edwina's, stocked and rotated on a schedule only she understands, kept the way Copper keeps his own. She can identify anything on the counter blind, by smell, from across the room, has opinions about the supplier she will share whether asked or not, and a memory for who has been shorted a delivery that the Counting House has never once needed to double-check. She is also small enough to hide in the gaps behind the shelving, which she does on purpose, to startle whichever neighbour has earned it that day.

The Cheese Festival empties the cold room onto trestles for one weekend a year, run between the two species who actually care about it: the Badgers carry and the Mice do the paperwork, and the paperwork is why it has happened every year without fail since anybody can remember.

places.name: The Gas Station
places.summary: Two pumps, a bell on the forecourt cable, and a bin emptied hourly.
paragraphs: Two pumps, a bell on the forecourt cable and a bin that is emptied hourly. Whatever the other town came in holding, some of it goes in that bin before they leave, and nobody has ever been able to say quite how.

Reese checks the City Dump before every trip, not for spares but for the lists — the manifests and the freight notes the Capital City throws out — on the grounds that a Raccoon reads the bins and the bins are where a borough says what it is actually doing. He would rather you thought it was instinct.

places.name: The Statues and the quarry
places.summary: Fifteen carved virtues, nine standing in any one year, and the rest still in the stone.
paragraphs: The Statues are the town's stated virtues. Nine stand in the Capital City in any one year — Kindness, Patience, Ingenuity, Curiosity, Generosity, Joy, Courage, Community and Harmony — and six more have been cut out of the same quarry over the years: Diligence, Hospitality, Vigilance, Wonder, Thrift and Mercy. The quarry still holds the rest, which is why two animals can honestly remember a different set and why which nine pass through the Capital City is not the same from one year to the next. Holding five wins the game; each grants a boon and imposes a burden.

The masons did not carve them in the abstract. Kindness holds a tray out at the height of a kitten and the square smells of Marmalade's ovens on a cold morning, which the mason did not plan and would not change. Curiosity has its eyes on the hill road, which is where Comet was looking the two times the board turned her down and the third time it did not. Community stands nine figures on one plinth, which is more than the commission asked for and exactly the number of Oatmeal's family. Diligence is carved mid-stride, one pace ahead of a row of four who are all looking at its back. Thrift has a full sack at its feet and its paw resolutely not on it. Mercy kneels with both paws busy and its face turned away from whoever is in them.

Getting one out of the quarry is its own business. The Masons' Rate arrives when the quarry has more stone cut than it has orders for. The quarry road goes out when the long pull to the county gate has gone in the wet, and nothing carved comes down it until it is made. And a Monument Tax arrives on the grounds that a borough rich enough to raise a monument is a borough rich enough to be asked about it.

boroughs.name: The Boroughs
boroughs.tagline: The First Boroughs: a young town still being built, with a plural in its name because this has happened before.

history.heading: A town still being built
paragraphs: The First Boroughs are not finished, and that is the single fact most of the town's character comes out of. It is why Barrow came out from the Capital City after twenty years cutting stone there: he wanted somewhere a wall he set this spring would still be the wall everybody walks past in thirty years, and somewhere the animals walking past it would know who set it. The borough was founded twice, they say — once on the hill, and once the spring Barrow stood up in front of everybody and said it was not finished.

A town can build for itself, and does. Alongside the Capital City's civic monuments the borough raises its own small places — a strip, a cellar, a bench, a shed, a gate — paid for by the Mayor and put up by animals taken off their work for a day or two to do it. They are permanent and personal, and a town has room for only so many of them, because the Statues stand in the same places. Each one already belonged to somebody before it was a place you could build.

It is also a town that keeps growing more work than it has names for. Food became a study when the café by the Hiring Hall turned into the place half the borough's business got done. Entertainment became a study because of what kept happening on the Festival Green after the shift ended, and its token was struck last of the eight.

history.heading: The bridge, the gates and what they cost
paragraphs: The year the bridge went is how animals here date things. Adam kept the carts moving the long way round for most of that spring at a cost of a day on every load, and has never claimed it as anything. Copper did not open the cellar under the weights office. Scott will not print a year Ned has not certified, so when Scott says which spring it was, the borough stops arguing about it. The other reference point is the winter the Grain Exchange shut for six weeks, and there has since been a frost that took the river hard from the ferry steps to the county line for five weeks.

Getting in and out of the borough has a price the rest of the year too. The county gate is shut from six and Bob does not care who you say you are, and the board by the bar has said pay it or work it off since before anybody currently arguing about it was born: the gate is the borough's and the tolls are the harbour office's. Finn had the keeping of the toll gate for a season, which is mentioned to nobody. The ferry has its tin — four crossings an hour and one more after the gate is shut for whoever is still on the wrong bank — and the tin fills on a busy night and does not on a quiet one, which is the whole of the ferry's accounts. Peanut keeps the books for those tolls along with the grange's feed bills and the guild's quarterly returns.

And the roads are their own toll. The long pull to the county gate is a quarter-hour shorter than the road it replaced, which was Adam's idea, and the cutting that made it shorter is the cutting that came down; he was up there with a lamp before the noise had finished and did not ask anybody to come with him.

history.heading: The wards, the board and the court
paragraphs: The borough is run in wards, and the paperwork is the part it is proudest of. Ned keeps the ward records and the records are right; Velvet keeps the building consents and reads every form aloud, slowly, all of it, and genuinely enjoys the queue. In fifteen years the two shelves have never disagreed. Both of the borough's standing arguments about the far hedgerow were settled out of Ned's shelves in an afternoon. Quinn is at the back of every meeting with the book open and says nothing at any of them.

Cindy sits in the ward court, one room over the old assize office with a window that does not shut and a bench somebody made too high, and the circuit takes her round the other three wards. Tax Day queues at the same office — Peanut has the desk and Cindy has the room next door for the grievances. Roger is made chair of everything because he can fix anything, and cannot decide, so an even call is settled by his ha'penny: somebody else throws it, never Roger, and whatever it does is what happens and he writes it down.

The board is the other half of ward life. Henrietta posts it and Nancy runs the temp board beside her; the Hiring Hall's second chances come back through Rosabeth's gate, Quill's orchard and Gwen's counter; and a lean season is a bare board by Tuesday rather than a disaster, carefully distinguished from the winter the Exchange shut and the year the bridge went, which were.

Ned's records also carry an unsigned column. When a post here is worked by an animal who gives no name, Ned will not leave the entry blank and will not invent one, so the record says what the ward saw. There are eighteen such standing entries, and almost always some animal the borough already knows turns out to have been the one standing there.

history.heading: Where the business actually gets done
paragraphs: Very little of the borough's business is done at a desk. Bean's café by the Hiring Hall is where the accounts are kept, the prices compared and the hiring gossiped about, and any character who works for wages has stood at that counter; Peanut does the accounts between orders and passes the good deals across with the change. Gwen's diner is on the square directly opposite, and the two counters have divided the borough's bad mornings between them without ever discussing it: at Bean's you find out there is nothing on the board, and at Gwen's you get a shift anyway.

Earl keeps the afternoons. His tea house is where an animal who needs to sit down with somebody sits down for two hours, and half the borough's apprentices have been talked into the next thing across that counter, usually over a pot they did not pay for. A good deal of the Auction House is settled over the second pot. He buys his leaf through Bean's supplier and the two of them have never competed for an hour.

After dark it moves again. Hazel's night market is where the town buys the things it cannot name, and it is the reason the night trade has a voice at daylight meetings at all. The Farmer's Market has the square on a Saturday from six until one and pays what the borough actually brought. And when the Capital City sends somebody out to do business, it is Finn who meets them, because he is the only animal in town who enjoys it.

history.heading: The night
paragraphs: The night is a real part of the town rather than an absence of the day: an observatory, an all-night café, a night school and Owls who work while the rest of the borough sleeps. Hoot keeps the ward's keys and the standing list of animals who have asked to be woken, and knocks at four in the morning on anybody on it — being woken here is a service you sign up for, not something that happens to you. The ward's night kitchen came after the list and for the same reason: if you are going to knock on a door at four in the morning you had better have something with you.

The lamps for the night round are filled at Benjamin's bench and nowhere else, which is his rule and not the ward's, and Mandee carries them; between the two of them the night shift has never stumbled. Marmalade bakes while the ovens are banked and hands it out in the morning, kittens first. Hazel's trestles go up when the lamps go on and come down around four. Taco's cart is open at four for the lightermen and shut at noon. Barnaby audits the night's books and is gone before the first shift bell. Andrew is at the Lending Library's late desk with a page and a half still to do.

The night also teaches. Jessica's night school starts at ten and has no homework, and the half of that room that is not kittens is animals already in a job who would like a better one; half the Hiring Hall's promotions these ten years started there. On a full moon the night round needs no lanterns, Benjamin fills them anyway, Hoot knocks the list an hour early, and everything in the borough that has been waiting for light gets done between midnight and four.

history.heading: Incorporations past
paragraphs: The borough has been incorporated before, and does not talk about it. Ned's shelves hold the closed charters: three of them, under names nobody in the First Boroughs uses out loud, two of which Scott has printed and Ned has certified.

Being incorporated is not remembered here as a defeat and is not remembered as a kindness either. It is remembered as the year the board changed and the work carried on: wards merged, two Hiring Halls putting up one board, and every animal keeping their work. Any animal old enough may have been on the wrong side of one, and the plural in the town's name is the only part of it anybody says out loud.

places.name: Bean's Café
places.summary: The counter by the Hiring Hall where the borough's accounts, prices and hiring all get discussed.
paragraphs: Bean's parents ran the coffeehouse by the Hiring Hall for thirty years and then retired to the tropics on a Tuesday with four days' notice. Bean was not consulted and has not stopped moving since: open before the early shift, still wiping down when the night workers come off, three orders behind and convinced the whole thing is about to come apart. It never quite does.

It is where the borough's accounts are kept, its prices compared and its hiring gossiped about, and any character who works for wages has stood at that counter. Peanut took the day counter mostly to have somewhere to spread the ledgers out, and discovered that if you give the whole town coffee they will tell you what everything costs. The accounts get done between orders and the good deals get passed across with the change. On quarter day half the borough's accounts pass over that counter. There is a penny jar on it that Peanut will not explain, emptied three times, always for somebody else, always the week they needed it.
Food is a study because of this room. It was named when the café became the place half the borough's business got done.

places.name: Gwen's Counter
places.summary: A griddle, a hatch, a row of stools, and an apron for anybody who asks.
paragraphs: A griddle, a hatch, a row of stools and an apron on a hook by the door. Gwen's diner is on the square at the Hiring Hall corner, directly opposite Bean's, and the two counters have divided the borough's bad mornings between them: at Bean's you find out there is nothing on the board, and at Gwen's you get a shift anyway.

Anybody who walks in and asks for work gets an apron that day, with no questions, no term and no mention of it afterwards. She pays at the end of the shift, in coin. It is the third of the borough's soft landings — Rosabeth's gate takes the animals who have stopped getting up, the orchard takes everybody all the time, and Gwen's pays you at the end of the shift — and the least sentimental of the three, because the griddle is hot and there is no time to feel anything about it until the rush is over. Half the borough has worked a fortnight here between one career and the next, and the borough has agreed without agreeing anything that a fortnight at Gwen's is not worth mentioning. The Hiring Hall has twice tried to make it a formal arrangement and twice been told it would ruin it.

Abigail has worked the counter since the week she turned up needing a fortnight between things and never left; she remembers an order without writing it down and the jar by the register has her name on it more often than the register does. Liza works it between bookings and sings while she does it, which Gwen permits on the grounds that the rush goes faster. Finn has had a turn at the griddle too.

places.name: The Tea House
places.summary: Earl's room, which keeps the afternoons.
paragraphs: The tea house keeps the afternoons and the café keeps the mornings. Earl's room is where an animal who needs to sit down with somebody sits down for two hours; Bean's counter has the accounts and the noise. They have never competed for an hour, and Earl buys his leaf through Bean's supplier.

There are two Earls and the difference between them is a pot of tea. The afternoon one listens for an hour without moving and says one thing at the end of it, and animals go away and act on the one thing. The one before the first cup is fast, loud and four jobs at once, halfway up a ladder with the urn in one paw. Both of them push animals up: he cannot watch somebody be good at a job and stay in it, and half the borough's apprentices have been talked into the next thing across his counter, usually over a pot they did not pay for. A good deal of the Auction House is settled over the second pot, and the Earl who is still pouring at two in the morning has heard everything worth hearing in the borough and is in no state to be anywhere at nine.

places.name: The Night Market
places.summary: Hazel's, which keeps its own hours and sells the things the town cannot name.
paragraphs: The trestles go up when the lamps go on and come down around four. It sets up after the gate is shut and packs before the gate is open, and it is where the town buys the things it cannot name: bottles with no labels, a drawer of keys to doors nobody can place, charts of a sky that is not quite this one, and reliably, unpredictably, the one thing you needed and could not have named.

It is Hazel's, and where any of it comes from is Hazel's business — the bins, the barges and the City Dump, first. What the day market cannot name comes on here from Tuppence's cart, because not being able to name a thing is the whole appeal. Hazel is back before the lamps go out with something the Capital City threw away and a straight face about where it came from.

It is also the reason the night trade has a voice at daylight meetings at all. Hazel has run the guild hall twice and sits on the market committee, and turns up to both in the coat they closed the stall in. Their position, given twice at committee and once at the guild hall, is that they take a pitch fee and not a pedigree, and that anybody who wants a name off her stallholders can come down at two in the morning and ask them — which is why the hedgehog with the scarf round her face on the cold end trestle, four winters running, is in the ward record and nowhere else.

places.name: The Community Oven
places.summary: Not a building anybody owns: the ovens are banked overnight and shared out by morning.
paragraphs: The borough's ovens are banked overnight and shared out by morning. The Community Oven is a standing arrangement rather than a building somebody owns, the account of who banked what is kept in chalk on the oven door, and it is the arrangement that made Food a study rather than a sideline of Commerce. Food pays for Food; it always has.

Marmalade has the night heat. He was a horrible kitten who was walked home by Biff more times than anyone has the heart to count, and then somebody put him in front of a bowl of dough to keep his paws busy and he was quiet for the first time in his life. He bakes three recipes nobody asked for by morning and hands half of it out before it is paid for, kittens first, because he knows precisely what a kitten with nothing to do turns into. On a Sunday he sets the long table down the middle of the room and the tray goes round the kittens first: nobody is hired at it and nobody is paid, they are simply fed, and on Monday they turn up.

Cookie takes the late heat after the bread is out and bakes for the Winter Stores. And for one winter somebody was at the hatch before Marmalade was with the trays already turned — a rabbit, hood up, out the side door the moment the queue started — which did not strike him as worth reporting and struck Ned as worth recording.

places.name: The Mill Kitchen
places.summary: The far end of the watermill, where Morty grinds it and then cooks it.
paragraphs: Morty keeps the watermill turning and dresses the stone twice a year, and will tell you at length that the mill is the wheel and not the building. He is right and it does not help. He built the boiler the Science hall said would not hold, and the annual boiler test is a borough fixture that the whole town attends and at which nothing has ever gone wrong, which Morty regards as the point and everybody else regards as a shame.

The kitchen is the other half of him. He grinds it and then he cooks it, and animals bringing grain to the mill have learned to turn up hungry. He and Marmalade trade recipes against repairs, and Morty takes notes on a recipe the way he takes notes on a bearing. Osh's eleven-day sharpening round has the mill kitchen and the bakery both on day four. Benjamin made Morty move the mill's spare oil.
On the nights Taco was up here trading recipes, the cart at the ferry steps stayed open with somebody else behind the hatch and did not move, which is the only thing about it anybody found strange.

places.name: The Orchard
places.summary: Quill's, from her parents, and it is never empty.
paragraphs: Quill's parents had the orchard and their parents before that, and Quill grew up under it in the long grass being handed windfalls. What she has decided, over and over, is that the rows should be full: there is a cider social in the barn from September to February and a bonfire whenever the prunings get above knee height, which is rather more often than pruning strictly requires. Half the borough has picked here one autumn and about a third of them turned up for a Saturday and were still there at the end of the week, on the books, being paid.

It is also the borough's quietest door back into work. Rosabeth's garden takes the animals who have stopped getting up; the orchard takes everybody, all the time, whether or not anything is wrong, so a hedgehog who is quietly out of work can be in the rows on a Saturday morning without ever having admitted to anything. The Hiring Hall knows and sends them. Quill pretends not to have noticed, hands them a basket, and puts the kettle on for thirty. When the Capital City stops signing and the first names come off the board, this is where they go.

The Harvest Fair runs the press all week and the barn holds thirty animals and a queue, and nobody has ever been turned away from it, which is why the neighbouring borough always comes off better than it should.

places.name: The Allotment Strip
places.summary: Four generations of one family's ground, and where half the borough's gardeners started.
paragraphs: Four generations of Clover's family have held this strip, and Clover is the first of them to write down what it does in a wet year. The family could all tell you what was wrong with a plant by looking at it and could not have told you why; Clover added the notebook, the labelled rows and the two identical beds planted differently on purpose to see what happened, which Clover's grandmother called fussing.

Clover has never once gone anywhere alone, and it is not nerves — it simply does not occur to them that a thing worth doing is worth doing by yourself. Half the borough's gardeners started as somebody Clover brought along to look at something, and every packet handed out on the strip at a seed drive comes back as a basket in the autumn, usually with the gardener attached.

The strip is not only Clover's. Teresa grows an unreasonable number of pepper varieties at the far end of it, the oak on the far side is standing today because a six-year-old Maribel sat in the roots of it for a day and a half while the grange argued overhead, and there is never one Bunny on the light rows — there is a Bunny and then five more coming round the end of the strip.

places.name: The Seed Bank
places.summary: Every variety the First Boroughs have ever grown, dried, doubled and labelled.
paragraphs: Maribel keeps the seed bank and the seed bank keeps the borough: every variety the First Boroughs have ever grown, dried, doubled and labelled, held against a bad year, and the labels are hers because she does not trust anybody else's. Clover's allotment strip has four generations behind it and Maribel has the seed stock for all four in a tin.

There is one open day a year. Maribel puts the drawers out on the trestles and nobody pays for a packet; you come back next autumn with two of them, and she writes that down. There is a line in the returns column that has been paid every autumn for eleven years with nothing in the name column — two packets, always, dry and clean and better than what went out — and Maribel, who files an objection twice and has it thrown out twice rather than leave a form unfinished, leaves that one.

She is also the animal who reads the whole ordinance before the meeting, finds the clause that saves the hedgerow and files the objection again on the Monday after it was thrown out on the Friday. She does not bid, does not enjoy being outbid, and would rather the town grew slowly and kept what it has, and will say so at length, in writing, on the record.

places.name: Rosabeth's Gate
places.summary: Where an animal who has stopped getting up is put back together, on the beds.
paragraphs: An animal who has lost a place and stopped getting up ends up at her gate, usually sent by somebody, and is put to work on the beds until they are fit to be somewhere else. Half the Hiring Hall's second chances started in that garden. She puts a mug of something in their paws and never tells them that is what is happening; she charges for the tincture and never for the rest of it.

The tinctures are the only remedies in the First Boroughs that reliably work. They are half herb and half whatever Rosabeth will describe as the moon, or the mood of the bed, or what the rosemary told her, and the Science hall has been through her notes twice and come away with a list of ingredients and no method. She says the method is the singing, which she has done out loud and in full view for thirty years; the borough stopped finding it strange in about the second decade and now regards it as weather. Betty gathers the material loudly and with a charge if the ground is difficult, and neither of them will say which half is the part that works.

The gate asks nothing of whoever is sent, which is the whole point of it, so a raccoon on the beds at six in the morning for most of one spring was not a thing anybody was going to interrupt. The far bed came in over that year, and so did the tinctures the Science hall failed to account for the second time.

places.name: The Surgery
places.summary: Shay's, two doors from the Physic Garden.
paragraphs: Shay keeps the surgery two doors from the Physic Garden, and Rosabeth's garden and the Science hall are on speaking terms because of her and not before her. She reads everything — the county papers, the Capital City's returns, the three medical journals that come up on the late ferry addressed to nobody in particular — and reads them the night they arrive, because she is an Owl and the night is when the reading gets done.

She does her rounds twice, and the second round crosses the ward boundary, because an animal asleep on their feet is an animal asleep on their feet whichever Mayor's town they happen to be standing in. It has been raised at three meetings and has never once been stopped.

The other half of her week is paint: small, quick, a great deal of green, taken to the Farmer's Market on a trestle with a price card on it next to Teresa's peppers. It is the only part of her life she will admit to doing badly, and she does it every week, which the borough has quietly noticed is what she tells everybody else to do.

places.name: The Clinic
places.summary: Two rooms, a scrubbed floor, and a coral tank in the waiting office.
paragraphs: Two rooms, a scrubbed floor and a coral tank in the waiting office that the babies of both boroughs will sit in front of for an hour. It is small, friendly and nobody's but the borough's, which is not a thing the borough can say about the Hospital. Whatever an animal came in unable to do, they generally go out able to do it.

JT works under Shay and ahead of her, in the way good nurses do: the small animals, the cheap hours, the ones who have not got a Supply to their name and turn up anyway. Nobody in the First Boroughs has put more animals back on their feet for less.

places.name: The Science Lab
places.summary: A bench and a bay FutureTech funds quietly, on the borough's own side of the water.
paragraphs: FutureTech funds it quietly, a floor below the Hospital's books and two above where anybody is allowed to ask questions, and the borough's own Science hall has stopped minding where the money comes from. It is kept separate from the Hospital's books and the Store's till, and the borough's Science-study animals work in it free of the Capital City's usual terms.

Cynthia's desk is in it. She is fascinated by science the way some animals are fascinated by a fire — completely, and occasionally at some risk to the furniture — and her desk did once catch fire three feet away from her without her noticing, because the experiment about how long a particular blue paint took to dry was a more interesting variable. The desk was replaced within the week; the story was not, and has been told at every open mic night since with a different ending depending on who is telling it. She keeps a jar of tokens on the bench, one for every experiment that comes to something, and trades them in for Supply when the budget runs thin.

places.name: The Science Hall
places.summary: The borough's own science, which asks Comet before it bids and files Bella's recordings.
paragraphs: The Science hall runs the Observatory's selection board with the Observatory, and it is the animal it asks before it bids on anything: Comet has read the Capital City's manifests, the dock lists and the Observatory's own order book, and knows what the Capital City is going to put up for sale before the Capital City has finished deciding. A lecture at the hall is Comet asking the question everyone else had decided not to ask, twice, and not being embarrassed either time.

Bella's field recordings are filed and cited here and have been for years, which is the borough's one piece of formal ecology; she has never bid on anything in the Capital City in her life. The hall has twice failed to account for Rosabeth's tinctures and has stopped writing it up, and it is on speaking terms with her garden because of Shay. It said Morty's boiler would not hold. It finds Juniper's habit of settling an even call by going outside and looking up maddening, and has had to concede that the calls come off.

The midges come off the water for three days most summers and stop everything, and the note the hall files on them every year is in two hands: one is Bella's, and the other has been turning up in the same folder for six years from a hide on the far bank that Bella did not build.

places.name: The Observatory Steps
places.summary: The borough's own way up to the dome, and what gets learned on the way.
paragraphs: Inkwell swept them for a season to be allowed up them and Comet read every book at the top before the board would look at her.
