Whoever is on the steps at four in the morning knows what is coming before the borough does. The telescope hire book is kept in Juniper's hand at the top of them, and Sota reseats the great brass one before letting anybody near it.

The steps are also the town's public sky. Sage's star party asks you to bring a blanket and a flask and on no account a lantern, and reads you the bit from the serial where the red world answers, and means every word of it. Sage has the eclipses to the minute eleven months out and the whole night class goes up the hill with smoked glass. Taco's cart moves to the top of that hill for the meteor shower, which is the one night of the year anybody can say in advance where the cart will be. And when a passing comet is announced the whole square goes out to lie on the cobbles, which is also when half the borough's best trades get agreed, because nobody haggles well looking up.

places.name: Berry's Bench
places.summary: Whatever the borough breaks ends up here, and so does whoever broke it.
paragraphs: Berry retired, and was back on the bench inside a fortnight. It starts small — somebody's hinge, somebody's pump — and by spring they are on the committee and by midsummer they are the one the Town Workshop calls when the Town Clock stops. They arrive with their own tools and a tin of something baked, work quietly and much faster than anyone expects, and will not hear a word about payment beyond the tea.

Tool lending day is a fixture and this bench is where it happens: half the borough's broken things queued along it and the other half out on loan. The rule of the bench is that the animal who brought the thing is the animal who mends it, with Berry on the second stool asking what they think is wrong with it, and still asking an hour later when they have fixed it. Younger animals come for the answer and leave having been walked into working it out themselves, which is a harder trick and takes longer, and Berry has all the time in the world for it. Moss was walked through his first joint here at twelve and Berry is still the one animal he listens to.

One tool lending day there was a badger on the second stool who was not Berry, in a work coat with the collar up, asking the same question in the same order. Berry was three streets away with the clock stopped and did not get back until dark, went along the row afterwards and said that whoever it was had done it properly.

places.name: Copper's Cellar
places.summary: Under the weights office, stocked since he was an apprentice and never once opened.
paragraphs: Copper keeps the borough's weights and measures, and under the weights office is a cellar he has been stocking since he was an apprentice: salt, lamp oil, candle stock and a shelf of small coin nobody has counted but Copper. It has never been opened. It was not opened the year the bridge went and it was not opened the winter the Grain Exchange shut for six weeks; both times he lent the salt out on the quiet, said this is bad and there will be worse, and did not touch the shelf.

This is not meanness — ask anyone he has quietly carried through a bad quarter. It is a settled conviction that something is coming and that somebody had better be ready. The Tax Assessors are the disaster it was stocked against and he has met them four times without once being surprised. What it makes him at the market is the cheapest animal in the borough to do business with: he has read every schedule of fees the Capital City prints and knows which can be got round, buys at the bottom of the day and rehires at the bottom of the month, and announces a price so mildly that the room takes a moment to notice it was a price.

He does a stocktake twice a year — everything out, everything weighed, everything written down, the useless half carried out to the yard — and is cheerful for a week afterwards. He also drew up the list the Winter Stores work from, and then built the one thing his own cellar has never had: a door somebody else is allowed to open.

places.name: Barrow's Yard
places.summary: Stone stacked by size, the good sand under a tarpaulin, and a Badger with opinions about foundations.
paragraphs: Stone stacked by size, the good sand under a tarpaulin, and a Badger who will tell you what a wall is worth whether or not you have asked. He bids on every lot that comes up with a roof on it, and he walks a lot before the auction, on his own, and comes back with a figure: the Capital City has never yet asked less than the figure and has never once been more than a Supply above it.

On the yard wall is a tin, and every chit in it is a lot Barrow has measured and priced and not bid on. He says the tin is the useful part. His Crafts token has his thumbprint pressed into the soft side of it, put there the day the borough struck them, because a thing worth making is worth knowing who made it, and he has more Building tokens than anyone in the borough and keeps them in the tin his father kept nails in.

He came out from the Capital City after twenty years cutting frontages and stairs, because the work there was too loud and too fast and the buildings were finished before he had finished looking at them. He is slow to talk and quick to help. He will not join the guild and turns up anyway. He costed the Builders' Rest, disapproved of it in writing, and eats his lunch in it.

places.name: The Builders' Rest
places.summary: Two benches, a tap and a roof, put up on the grounds that there had now been three jobs.
paragraphs: Two benches, a tap and a roof, put up by Moss on the third job on the grounds that there had now been three. Barrow costed it, disapproved of it in writing, and eats his lunch in it.

It is a fair example of how Moss works: he reads the sheet, puts it down, does the thing that works and lets the result argue. It has cost him two commissions and a formal warning from the Capital City, and it has given the borough a plough hitch that does not foul, a bridge arch a third lighter than the drawing, and a bench jig half the Town Workshop now uses without knowing whose it was.

places.name: The Muster Bell
places.summary: Rung once at the top of the shift and never for anything else.
paragraphs: Rung once at the top of the shift and never for anything else, which is why the borough can tell the time by it and why Adam will not have it rung for a road closure. The town bell proper is rung at six and at six, and once in between for something the borough will talk about for a year, and every apprentice in the wards can tell the difference in their sleep.
The yard has a horn as well as a bell, and the yard's oldest arrangement goes with it: whoever answers it second is working with whoever answered it first, and that is the whole of the rota.

places.name: The Long Awning
places.summary: Run the length of the square the spring the yards went short, and never taken down.
paragraphs: Oatmeal got the ward office to run it the length of the square the spring the yards went short, and the households that came through that spring unbothered were the ones he got to first. It has never been taken down.

He is the oldest of nine and it shows in everything he does: he counts heads at the door, and the head count does not stop at the ward boundary. The rival Mayor gets an animal under the awning too, which Oatmeal regards as the whole point and the ward office regards as a filing problem.

places.name: The Quill Wall
places.summary: Not much of a wall. Nothing has ever got over it.
paragraphs: Bob leans on it, Biff walks past it four times a night, and Berry mended the gate in it twice without being asked. It is not much of a wall. Nothing has ever got over it.

Biff polices the borough by knowing everyone on it: he stops the trouble, walks the troublemaker home, and a week later has found them something to do. The beat has the lowest trouble in the First Boroughs and he does not think it is because of anything clever he did. An animal who has been in trouble here has been walked home, not taken away.

places.name: The Gate Hut
places.summary: A bar, a lamp, and a hedgehog asleep behind both.
paragraphs: The county gate is shut from six and Bob does not care who you say you are. It is a post nobody else would take, because its whole duty is saying no, and Bob is immovable, unembarrassable, and can say no in his sleep, which is the arrangement the county and Bob have quietly come to. Carters who arrive at the wrong hour find the bar down and a hedgehog folded against it like a dropped coat.

The difficulty is the other half of the job. A gate has to open as well, and Bob is unbeatable at keeping the borough out and only intermittently good at letting it back in; there is a standing complaint at the Hiring Hall about the mail cart and three separate ones about the fish, and none of them has ever come to anything, because everyone who has tried to get past him at night agrees that nobody else could have kept them out either. He is Biff's opposite number in every way that matters: Biff's whole method is knowing everyone on his beat, and Bob's is not caring who you say you are.

The tolls are collected here and the board by the bar says pay it or work it off. Hoglets are put on the gate step, which is the safest place in the borough and the one where you learn the most, because everybody comes past the gate.

places.name: The Warren
places.summary: Nobody built it and nobody can say how far back it goes.
paragraphs: Nobody built it and nobody can say how far back it goes. Clover's family came out of one end of it and Lynnette's press sits over the other, and on any given morning there are more rabbits in it than were in it last night.

Two rabbits is a conversation; two rabbits and a notice on the Lending Library door is nine of them on the step by Thursday, and one of them already holding a tool. Henrietta knows every warren, every cousin and every animal who owes another animal a favour, and when a good job comes through the door she works the whole room until the hire happens. Jake runs the warren's long errands — the far rows, the sacks at the wrong end of the borough at the wrong end of the night — and has run them twice and left twice, and the Hiring Hall's position is that there will be a third time and that they will hire him for it.

places.name: The Print Shop and the Chit Press
places.summary: Lynnette's press, which everything printed in the First Boroughs these fifteen years has come off.
paragraphs: Lynnette got the press cheap because it was broken and learned to mend it because nobody else would, which is roughly her whole biography. The paper, the ballots, the almanac, the hymn sheets, the notices and every book printed in the First Boroughs these fifteen years have come off it, usually late and always right. What she actually loves is the spreading: the apprentice notices in the Hiring Hall, the guild's syllabus and the almanac's planting tables are hers, given free, and they are why an animal here can find out how to be better at their job without knowing anybody first.

The chits are struck here too. The ferry's family struck their own fare chits seven generations ago — a worn wooden otter on a round of hard wood — and everything the borough has stamped since is a copy of them, off this press, in the same hard wood. The building mark is struck twice a year and Velvet reads the consents aloud over the top of it, slowly, all of it, and genuinely enjoys the morning.

Everything Scott prints about a real animal or a real year goes across Ned's shelves first, and Ned certifies it or Scott cuts it; in fifteen years Lynnette has never had to print a correction to a word of his. Robbie's four sheets and a Thursday come off the same press. Orien supplies the almanac's figures and Lynnette sets the tables, and nobody in the borough has paid for a figure since. She keeps Kevin a shelf and has never charged him for a novel, and has offered Beck one for years, which he has never taken.

places.name: The Open Mic Room
places.summary: Whatever room will have them, a night a week, and Cassadee deciding which room.
paragraphs: Open mic nights happen in whatever room will have them and are a fixture of the town's evenings rather than a rarity. Cassadee decides which room: she books it, sweeps it, sets the chairs, finds the lamp oil, stands at the back with the list, and puts the chairs away again at midnight. She does not sing, play, recite or juggle and has turned down every invitation to try. Balto built the long table in it, uncommissioned, the way he builds everything.

Oatmeal's band is on her list more often than anybody's — four of his own brothers and sisters and a Fox on the piano — and Harrison, who cannot read a note, can follow an animal who has never rehearsed and is a half-step ahead by the second verse. Lynnette printed a paragraph about that once and it hangs at the back of the room where he cannot see it from the stool. Liza comes on her own with nothing and sings for twenty minutes to a room that stops moving, and has never been paid more than the hat. Abigail taps for five minutes on a slow night between the acts that actually rehearse. Yellow raps about the seed bank's open day and about pecan pie. Fred has been backstage crew for exactly one show he was never told the name of, and Tabitha shoots the room from a stool at the back.

The hat goes round at the end, comes back heavier than the set was worth, and Cassadee puts the chairs away. There is one recurring entry on her list with no name, given a slot on the same evening of the month for two years, always last, always after the room has thinned — and one night she was ill, came in anyway, and found the chairs stacked, the lamps out and the floor swept.

places.name: The Puppet Booth
places.summary: It folds flat and goes home on Gabe's back.
paragraphs: It folds flat and goes home on Gabe's back, and it has stood in the children's corner, the bakery queue and every late room Cassadee has ever given away. The cast is about forty now and they all have names, made out of the third pile at the Salvage Yard — what Patch has looked at and put down.

The shows are free and there are three regular ones: Saturday mornings in the Lending Library's children's corner, which is the slot Inkwell and Lynnette do not use; the bakery queue on the mornings Marmalade is handing out to the kittens first, which is a captive audience and Marmalade has never objected; and whatever room Cassadee will give him, late, when the list has run short. The children's version and the late version are not the same show and the borough has noticed.

places.name: The Farmer's Market
places.summary: Trestles on the square from six, down by one, paying what the borough actually brought.
paragraphs: Trestles on the square from six and down by one. Teresa's peppers are at the far end next to Shay's paintings and the two of them have never agreed about the pricing. It is a Town Building — the borough raises it for itself — and it pays what the borough actually brought, which on a thin week is nothing much and on a full one is the best morning of the month.

Marmalade works the stall in the day and cannot keep a queue moving to save his life, since everybody in it wants to tell him something. Hazel is here in daylight as well as at four in the morning. Clover sells out of the allotment strip, and Daisy's flowers come out of what she dried and put by in the quiet months.

places.name: The Grocery Store
places.summary: A plain one, older than any of the Capital City's newer lots.
paragraphs: Nothing about it is remarkable, which is rather the point: bread, milk, a till that adds up, and a queue that never once talks about the Capital City. It is older than any of the newer lots and owned by nobody in particular.

places.name: The Ice Cream Shop
places.summary: Run to the inch by four teenagers who have never met the owner.
paragraphs: Owned by an old Raccoon who retired to the arctic and never quite got round to selling it, and run to the inch by four teenagers who have never met him. Half the other town is in the queue on a warm afternoon and none of them are at work.

places.name: The Boat Shed
places.summary: Down past the ferry steps, kept by the lightermen.
paragraphs: Down past the ferry steps, where the lightermen keep what the harbour office would rather not know about. It is not strictly the harbour office's business, and Brooke has had a key for eight years.

Brooke went onto the dock rope gang at fourteen and has been working her way up the river trade ever since — dock hand, ferry hand, lighterman, wright — and cannot hear about a thing without going to find out how it is done. Somebody said once that she would never understand a hull until she had built one, so she built one; it took four years, it is still on the water, it is the best boat on the river, and it put her licence back by four years.

places.name: The Ferry Steps and the crossing
places.summary: Seven generations of one family, four crossings an hour, and a cart that keeps the river's hours.
paragraphs: The crossing has been Pebble's family's for seven generations, and the borough long ago stopped bothering with the names: whoever is on the boat is the ferryotter. Four crossings an hour, the same bank, the same rope, the same eleven regulars and their eleven opinions, and one more crossing after the gate is shut for whoever is still on the wrong bank. The tin fills on a busy night and does not on a quiet one, which is the whole of the ferry's accounts. Most families with a thing like that behind them produce somebody who wants out; Pebble's family has been waiting three generations for that animal and it is not going to be Pebble.

The chits are the other half of it. That family struck its own fare chits — a worn wooden otter on a round of hard wood, handed over at one bank and counted back at the other — and half the borough has one in a pocket it never handed back, and every one of them is still good. The rest of the town's chits, the study marks and the building mark, are copies of the ferry's.

There is a cart at the steps that keeps the river's hours and not the town's: Taco's, shut at noon and open at four in the morning, and never twice in the same place. Any lighterman coming off a night run has eaten there. Adam mends the lane down to the steps. And when somebody goes in off the steps, there is no otter in either borough doing the thing they were doing within the hour.

places.name: The Harbourmaster's Office
places.summary: Willow's desk, and the top of the river trade's ladder.
paragraphs: Willow started at nineteen with one bad ferry on terms its previous owner described for years as generous of him, and she signs now for everything that floats between the ferry steps and the county line, and for the boat yard, the towpath cottages and the arcade lease besides. She is the Harbourmaster, which is why the River Otter licence is granted out of this office and why the river trade's whole ladder — dock hand, ferry hand, lighterman, wright — runs up to her desk.

River Otter is a rank, not a species: the river trade's top licence, the animal permitted to take a loaded boat down the whole river alone, on its own word. Brooke has been about two years off it for eight years. Dylan has held it since he was absurdly young by means he has never stated — he answers the question with a story instead, and the story changes — and comes up the river on no schedule, is hired by the day, and is gone inside a week; asked plainly for help he gives it and gives it well, which is the one reliable fact about him.

Willow is the best talker in the First Boroughs and the borough is proud of her for it the way you are proud of weather. She does not lie and does not bully; she arrives having already worked out the two worst outcomes available to you, sets them both down with enormous warmth, and waits. The arcade counter under her lease wanted covering for a fortnight once and somebody covered it, correct to the halfpenny, and went on the Friday without collecting the last three days' wages.

places.name: The Airfield
places.summary: One strip and a windsock, up past the far field.
paragraphs: The airfield is one strip and a windsock, up past the far field. Reese flies out of it and Mimi runs everything about it that is not flying. An animal off the morning aircraft is standing in your town by nine and gone by supper, and the borough has decided that a day is a day.

Reese came up the way Raccoons come up, which is out of the yard: the first aircraft he ever touched was three aircraft and none of the three had all of its parts, and he can still tell you what came off which. He holds the borough's only instrument ticket and is the one who goes when the weather has shut the ferry. Mimi is the safety demonstration, the trolley, the pressure check, the welcome at the front step and the animal who settles the bill at the far end, and she flies with him most weeks. The sunglasses do not work on her, and she has never told him so.

places.name: The Ward Court
places.summary: One room over the old assize office, a window that does not shut and a bench somebody made too high.
paragraphs: Cindy sits in it, and the circuit takes her round the other three wards. She came up through it the long way — usher, clerk, magistrate — and has heard every version of every story the First Boroughs has to tell, most of them twice and a good many from the same animal on two different days. What she is known for is the stare: she asks a question and then waits, and does not fill the silence and does not look away, and the borough's own view is that nobody has ever got a lie all the way across that bench. She will not have a smart mouth, and she is fair, which in a Fox is the thing the borough finds hardest to credit and the thing she is proudest of.

A fair hearing here is Biff giving his account, which takes a while because he starts with everyone's names, and Brett reading the clause, and the animal in the dock walking out with a job, which is how it usually goes. Tax Day queues at the same office one morning a year with a tin and a grievance: Peanut has the desk and Cindy has the room next door for the grievances. Fingers has run errands for the court, in between mending locks for the Salvage Yard and turning up on a root-cellar job for the grange.

places.name: The Ward Office
places.summary: Ned's shelves, Velvet's counter, and the coin that settles an even call.
paragraphs: Ned keeps the ward record and the record is right: every ward roll, every guild return, every date the bridge was out and every name on the hiring list since before Ned was born, filed and cross-referenced, because a record that is nearly correct is a record that will one day be quoted by somebody who is nearly wrong. Both of the borough's standing arguments about the far hedgerow were settled out of those shelves in an afternoon. Velvet keeps the consents at the counter next door and reads every form aloud, slowly, all of it, and in fifteen years the two shelves have never disagreed. Moss's formal warning from the Capital City came across that counter, read aloud at the same pace to a badger who wanted to be anywhere else in the world.

Quinn is at everything with the book open and says nothing, and when a place falls vacant the Hiring Hall comes to him and he turns back four years and hands over a slip with a name on it. Roger is made chair of everything and cannot decide, so an even call is settled by his ha'penny — somebody else throws it, never Roger, on the grounds that calling it would be taking a side — and it has settled four boundary questions, a dispute about a bandstand, and who was to have the good pitch at the fair. Beck clerks the ward book, lights nothing on fire and is home by seven. Oatmeal works the safety notices and the register of who lives where.

There is an unsigned column in the record. When a post here is worked by an animal who gives no name, Ned will not leave the entry blank and will not invent a name for it, so the record says what the ward saw: the masked otter, the hooded rabbit, the clerk at the second window. There are eighteen such standing entries, and almost always some animal the borough already knows turns out to have been the one standing there, and the record is corrected to their name — which is a correction and not a promotion, and Ned files it as one. The shelf also carries eleven of Dirt's figurines, one of them labelled DIRT and unmistakably Squirt, uncorrected in four years.

places.name: The Borough School
places.summary: Two rooms, an upper and a lower, and it is not the night school.
paragraphs: The borough school is two rooms, an upper and a lower, and it is in the morning and has a bell. Dirt has the upper room and the longer patience — he is the one who will let a bad answer sit in the air for a while, which the kittens find unbearable and which works. Squirt has the lower room, the shorter fuse and the better legs, and is out of the door at the bell because the borough side trains at five.

Dirt and Squirt swap: on Tuesdays, mid-lesson, and twice during a ward meeting while a motion was being read. The swapping is mostly Squirt's idea and starts about ten minutes into something he has decided is boring. The borough has stopped trying to tell which of them is in which room, and the joke has been running so long it has become a sort of civic weather.

Jessica teaches the little ones here as well, in songs, games and activities, in that order, and has never once set homework — she agreed at a meeting some years ago that it was a very good idea and said she would think about it. The kittens can name every constellation and cannot spell any of them.

places.name: The Night School
places.summary: Jessica's, at ten at night, with no homework and half the Hiring Hall's promotions.
paragraphs: The night school is Jessica's and there is no homework. She teaches in songs, games and activities, has never once set any, and told a meeting some years ago that she would think about it. Tonight: fractions, the constellations, and why you should have gone to bed.

The other half of that room is not kittens. It is animals already in a job who have worked out they would like a better one, and Jessica is the one who finds the next rung and talks them onto it before they have finished explaining why they could not possibly. Half the Hiring Hall's promotions in the last ten years started in that room, at ten at night. She is small, extremely loud, and has never once been to bed before four.
It is also the class that goes up the hill with smoked glass when Sage has an eclipse to the minute eleven months out, which is the sort of homework Jessica does set.

places.name: The Night Kitchen
places.summary: Off the night round, with a bell on it and a rota.
paragraphs: The ward has a night kitchen off the night round, with a bell on it and a rota, and it is Hoot's. It came the same way the list of everybody's names did, which is to say nobody asked for it: if you are going to knock on a door at four in the morning you had better have something with you, so Hoot started carrying something and then started making it.

The job proper is night porter — doors, lamps, deliveries, the ward's keys, and getting up the animals who have asked to be got up. There is a standing list of animals who have asked to be woken, Hoot keeps it along with the keys, and knocks at four in the morning on anybody on it; being woken in the First Boroughs is a service you sign up for, not something that happens to you, and Hoot has never once been late with one. The list has what each of them takes in the morning written beside it, and Hoot has never once had to look.

Nobody signs up to have the sash cord replaced while they sleep, and yet: a sash cord, a dropped gate hinge, a pump handle, a stair tread, each done overnight in a ward where somebody had complained about it out loud the previous day. Berry says the work is good and that it is not hers. Moss says it is not his either, and that whoever it is does not foul a hitch.

places.name: The Fairground
places.summary: The fair, its warden, and the booth with a queue that starts before she does.
paragraphs: The fair has a warden and the warden is Finn, who has also had, and lost, a weighing job at the Grain Exchange and a season on the toll gate. The borough knows exactly where he sits between honest and otherwise, has known since he was about nine, and puts him on the committee anyway. He keeps the fair's weights honest and remembers vividly what the Finn of five years ago would have done with them, and he is who meets the Capital City's traders when they come out, because he is the only animal in town who enjoys it.

Elvira's booth is here most weeks, with a roof on it now and a queue that starts before she does. She reads futures, is right often enough that the borough has stopped being able to laugh it off and wrong often enough that nobody can quite call it a trade. What she is never wrong about is the mood: she reads for animals who have had a hard season and sends them out of the booth better than they came in, which she will tell you cheerfully is the actual job.

The fairs themselves come in sizes and they all want paying. There is a small fair of three stalls and a rope ring where the toll man stands at the gate all the same; a county fair where every stall in the borough turns up at once and every one of them wants paying; a midsummer fair with the longest day and the longest queue at the gate; and, once a generation, a Lord Mayor's Fair that the whole borough turns out for, which is exactly the trouble. Roger's ha'penny settled who was to have the good pitch at one of them.

places.name: The Square
places.summary: The Town Clock, the trestles, the cobbles, and everything the borough does out of doors.
paragraphs: The Town Clock's hour is the hour it is: brass gears, exposed on purpose, and a face the whole square sets its morning by. When it stops the borough calls Berry, and Berry answers to the Town Workshop about it afterwards, and nobody has ever proposed a second clock. The market committee sits over the guildhall here with a cat for a weathervane that nobody will admit to paying for.

The square is where the trestles go up on a Saturday, where Daisy's garlands go up for festival week, where the awning runs the whole length, and where Adam has the cobbles up after festival week and will not be hurried about it — which is how the Capital City once discovered it had nowhere to put a monument. Hibiscus's round starts from the sorting bench at five and ends about seven hours later with half the lane out of doors behind it.

The Car Show is held here on market day because the square is already full, and both boroughs turn out. And when somebody with a chart says a comet is passing, by ten the whole square is out on its back on the cobbles: Sage counts them aloud, everybody quietly fetches the one card they have been waiting on, and half the borough's best trades get agreed flat on a cold night. The year the square was quiet and the reading room was full is the one Ned can give you the date for, and the order the boards came down in, and the morning each one went back up.

places.name: The Far Field, the hedgerows and the grange
places.summary: The borough's working ground, and where it does its remembering.
paragraphs: The grange sends Thistle out at the head of a row with the animals who are sure they are no good at it, because the row keeps his pace: he has never once looked back, and an animal who falls in behind him comes off the field having done half again what they meant to and does not feel it until morning. It works about nine times in ten. There is always a chair at the long table of his grange supper for somebody who has been away, and he sets it, sits at the far end and says nothing for two hours. The borough's wage rates are compared against Eric's, who can say to the Supply what an animal costs to keep for a season and will say it out loud in front of them, and pays the figure he says.

Betty is who the grange sends for when a field has to be cleared, with a charge and an afternoon rather than a season with a mattock; the same powder supplies Blossom Week's finale, so the borough's fireworks and its stump-clearing come off the same bench. The reclaimed strip along the far hedgerow is hers — four seasons of work, the best ground in the borough, and already sold on. The hedges themselves are laid rather than planted and Peter lays them: cut most of the way through, bent over living, pegged down, and fifteen years before anybody knows whether he did it properly. That is the other half of why a hedgerow here is hard to take down — Maribel files the objection, Peter grew the wall.

The far field is also where the borough does its remembering. The Community Bonfire is one night a year: the year's broken pallets go on, the animals who keep the records do the talking, Ned brings the ward book and Lynnette brings the water-stained novels nobody has wanted since the bridge went, and the other borough walks over the hill for it and is handed a chair.

places.name: The Long Pull to the County Gate
places.summary: A quarter-hour shorter than the road it replaced, and the cutting that made it shorter came down.
paragraphs: The borough's roads are Adam's — the ferry steps lane, the long pull up to the county gate, the square's cobbles after festival week — and all of it is work nobody notices until it stops being done. The pull is a quarter-hour shorter than the road it replaced, which was his idea. He lays the level across the surveyor's table and the whole county gate road comes off the same sheet, and a town that has built before does not pay what a town that has not pays.

The cutting that made it shorter is the cutting that came down. Adam was up there with a lamp before the noise had finished and did not ask anybody to come with him. He was out on this road the year the bridge went as well, for most of that spring, keeping the carts moving the long way round at a cost of a day on every load.
It is the road the quarry uses. When the pull goes in the wet, nothing carved comes down it until it is made, and everybody knew that before they started arguing.

places.name: The City Dump and Unemployment
places.summary: Where cards and animals go when work runs out. Both are ordinary parts of town life.
paragraphs: The City Dump and Unemployment are where cards and animals go when the work runs out, and the borough is clear that neither is a disgrace. A town holds ten animals at a time — at work, pledged into an auction, or face down in Unemployment — so a spell down there is arithmetic rather than a verdict.

The Dump has its own economy. Pockets works it the way his brother works the Salvage Yard, except that Patch sells you back your own mangle, mended, and Pockets sells you somebody else's and does not say whose; nothing he does is quite a crime and several things are the shape of one, seen from a distance, in poor light. Hazel gets there first, and is back before the lamps go out with something the Capital City threw away and a straight face about where it came from. Raccoon Kits carry the shelf's stock up one piece at a time. Beck takes a split almanac off it and reads it by candlelight. Benjamin works it the way other animals work a shelf, because a thing thrown out is a thing somebody decided about. Reese checks it before every trip, for the lists rather than the spares.

Getting back out of Unemployment is the borough's most practised trade. Nancy's temp board can have an animal off it by Wednesday. Quinn turns back four years in a lean season and hands out slips with names on them. Rosabeth's gate, Quill's orchard and Gwen's counter take the ones who are not ready to say so. And a redundancy notice here is a single sheet, correctly worded, served at the end of the shift so that nobody has to stand about afterwards, with the last wages paid out in full and in coin and everybody walked to the door rather than left to find it.

relationships.text: Bean owns the café; Peanut runs its counter. Bean inherited it, Peanut keeps the books, and on the days Bean is coming apart Peanut quietly takes over. Peanut does not own it and has never wanted to.

Bob and Betty are twins, born the same wet morning at the far end of the borough, and are as unlike as two hedgehogs can be: Bob stops, Betty goes. Between them they were issued exactly one animal's worth of energy and Betty took it. They are on good terms and see each other rarely, which both regard as the natural order.

Rosabeth sings to her plants, out loud, in full view, and has for thirty years. The borough stopped finding it strange in about the second decade and now regards it as weather. She says the singing is the method.
Peanut keeps the books for half the borough: the grange's feed bills, the ferry's tolls, the guild's quarterly returns. A character with accounts has plausibly had them audited, kindly, by Peanut.
Lynnette keeps Kevin a shelf at the print shop. He reads four or five novels at once through the flat fortnight between jobs, and she has never charged him for one.

Beck takes what the borough throws out. He reads by candlelight every evening — split almanacs, water-stained novels, ward minutes nobody has wanted since the bridge went — and Lynnette has offered him a shelf at the print shop for years, which he has never taken. He prefers the ones nobody else wanted.

Inkwell is widely rumoured to be a mage and has never once denied it. Nobody has anything better than the rumour, and the borough is content with that. What is true is that things go slightly still around them and animals who meant to leave an hour ago find that they have not.

Patch and Pockets are brothers, and Pockets is the older one who taught Patch to dive. Patch built a yard, a counter and a price list out of it; Pockets got range instead, and works the City Dump and the Capital City's gate for things nobody will ask the history of. Pockets turns up at the yard about four times a year, is fed, and leaves with something, and Patch has never once asked what for.

Lindsay and Rosabeth are the borough's two impossible gardeners. Rosabeth sings to her plants in full view and has for thirty years; Lindsay is not there at all, waters the whole bench without noticing, and cannot afterwards tell you what she did. Both sets of beds come in over, and the borough has stopped expecting gardening to make sense.

The borough's children are certain Quinn is a mage, on the grounds that the writing comes out faster than the talking goes in, and that he was seen at the fair, the regatta and the Hiring Hall on one afternoon. Inkwell, asked once to settle it, said only that Quinn writes faster than he does.

Thistle is at the open mic on the nights one particular singer is on the list. He is at the back by the door, does not take his coat off, listens to the one set with his eyes shut and is gone before the applause. Cassadee keeps the list, knows exactly which nights he comes, has twice moved that singer up the running order so he would not have to stay so late, and has never mentioned any of it to him. The borough gossips about this and only this, and does it very quietly.

The singer Thistle comes for is Liza, who has been on Cassadee's list since she was seventeen, comes on her own with nothing, sings for twenty minutes to a room that stops moving, and has never been paid more than the hat. She has turned the Festival Green down twice on the grounds that it is too big a room to be honest in. She does not know about Thistle, and Cassadee has never told her.

Sage and Sota work the same bench for whole nights without either saying anything the other wants to hear. Sota grinds the lenses and has no interest in what they are pointed at; Sage is the opposite animal. Neither has ever suggested a different arrangement.

Pebble's family will not meet Willow without a third animal present. It is a standing rule, seven generations into holding the crossing, and they will not say which year they made it. Willow has offered Pebble the warden's post three times, and Pebble took it on the third offer on the condition that it did not mean giving up the boat.

Velvet genuinely enjoys the queue. He said in a public meeting that the small talk while a long form is filled in is the best part of his week. The borough was startled, thought about it, and decided to believe him.

Dirt and Squirt swap. On Tuesdays, mid-lesson, and twice during a ward meeting while a motion was being read. The borough has stopped trying to tell which of them is in which room, and Ned's shelf carries a figurine labelled DIRT that is unmistakably Squirt and has not been corrected in four years.

Bob keeps the county gate and the county gate is shut from six. He is Biff's opposite number in every way that matters: Biff's whole method is knowing everyone on his beat, and Bob's is not caring who you say you are. Both of them are immovable about it and both of them are right about their own half of the job.

Berry walked Moss through his first joint when he was twelve and has been the one animal Moss will listen to ever since. What Berry actually taught him, Moss will tell you, was not the joint — it was that you work it out yourself, which is exactly what the guild now finds so annoying.

River Otter is a rank, not a species: the river trade's top licence, granted out of the Harbourmaster's office, with a ladder that runs dock hand, ferry hand, lighterman, wright. Dylan has held it since he was absurdly young by means he has never stated. Brooke has been about two years off it for eight years, and has met him twice, and took notes both times.

Annabelle pulls the paper out of the Salvage Yard before the weather gets at it and keeps what has words on it; Beck gets first read of anything with a story in it. It is an arrangement of long standing and no written terms, and neither of them has ever said it out loud.

The Salvage Yard is divided without anybody having said so. Annabelle takes the paper; Patch takes everything else and sells it back to the borough mended or improved; Gabe takes what Patch has looked at and put down and makes puppets out of it, about forty now, all named. What Patch will not take, Pockets will, and does not say whose it was. Gabe is not Patch's brother — Pockets is — but he turns up about as often, is fed, and leaves with something.

Morty and Marmalade trade recipes against repairs: a recipe for a mended oven door, and Morty takes notes on the recipe the way he takes notes on a bearing. Osh's sharpening round takes eleven days and has gone in the same order since he was a kitten, and the mill kitchen and the bakery are both on day four.

Barrow and Brett are the same big city and the opposite decision. Barrow came out from the Capital City after twenty years cutting stone and stayed, because the Boroughs are not finished being built. Brett practises there, comes out when the borough needs somebody who knows how the Capital City's rules are written, and goes home the same evening. The Counting House budgets for him a year ahead.

The borough's hedges are laid, not planted, and Peter lays them — cut most of the way through, bent over living, pegged down, and fifteen years before anybody knows whether he did it properly. Maribel reads the whole ordinance before the meeting and files the objection again after it is thrown out. Maribel files the objection; Peter grew the wall. The two of them have never discussed it.

Ned keeps the ward records and Velvet keeps the consents; they are different shelves, and in fifteen years the two have never disagreed, which both of them regard as ordinary and everybody else regards as slightly eerie. Moss's formal warning from the Capital City came across Velvet's counter and was read aloud, at the same pace as everything else.

Everything Scott prints about a real animal or a real year goes across Ned's shelves first, and Ned certifies it or Scott cuts it; in fifteen years Lynnette has never printed a correction to a word of his. The other half of his shelf is invention and is not kept separate from it. When Scott says the bridge went in a particular spring, the borough stops arguing about which spring.

Oatmeal is the oldest of nine and four of his brothers and sisters play in his band; the Fox on the piano is Harrison, who is on the piano in everybody else's band too and cannot read a note. Cassadee books them more often than anybody, which she says is because they turn up on time. Oatmeal's family has never missed a show.

The tea house keeps the afternoons and the café keeps the mornings. Earl's room is where an animal who needs to sit down with somebody sits down for two hours; Bean's counter by the Hiring Hall has the accounts and the noise. They have never competed for an hour, and Earl buys his leaf through Bean's supplier.

The borough has three doors back into work and has never called them that. Rosabeth's gate takes the animals who have stopped getting up and sets them on the beds; Quill's orchard takes everybody, all the time, so that nobody has to admit to anything; and Gwen's hands you an apron and pays you at the end of the shift. Gwen's is the least sentimental of the three, and the Hiring Hall has twice tried to make it formal and twice been told it would ruin it.

Hibiscus walks the borough's round and Juniper carries what leaves it, and the two of them hand over at the sorting bench at five every morning. Nothing on that round is ever lost and the round takes seven hours, because Hibiscus cannot be got off a doorstep in under ten minutes. The standing complaints about the late second post are filed next to the ones about the county gate.

The borough has two animals it does not ask about, and has decided not to compare notes. Barnaby audits the Capital City's night books and has no address on file. Mandee works nights only, is not on Hoot's waking list, has a blank address line at the Hiring Hall, and twice an animal who set out to walk home with her found they were walking home alone. Scott keeps a whole shelf of her tales, files it with the invention, and has said once, not as a joke, that he is not sure that is the right shelf.

Sota has taken on more than one apprentice at the lens bench, and not always ones bound for the sky: Tabitha spent two winters there arguing about focal length and came away able to say exactly why a lens does what it does, which she now turns on cameras rather than telescopes.

The Observatory's selection board has turned down more than one applicant it later leaned on anyway. Comet got in on her third try; Winter never did, and ended up reading the manifests, the order book and the launch windows for a different room entirely.

Roger has twice asked another animal to be the one who calls his ha'penny in the air, on the grounds that even the coin needs a hand that is not his, and been refused both times. Fred refused on the grounds that even that felt like too much responsibility.

The Grain Exchange's weighbridge is Liz's: every loaded cart in or out of the borough crosses her plate and is paid on what she writes. Copper's office certifies the bridge each spring and has never had to adjust it. It is the weighing job Finn had and lost, which the borough mentions to neither of them.

The almanac's price tables are Orien's figures. He keeps a calculating engine in his back room, built out of Observatory cast-offs and whatever Patch would sell him, and feeds it the shift returns, the auction prices, the ferry's crossings and the weighbridge's plate. Lynnette sets the tables and nobody in the borough has paid for a figure since. Ask him what a Building will go for and he will be within a Supply.

The night round's lanterns come off Benjamin's bench and Mandee carries them, and between the two of them the night shift has never stumbled. Filling them at his bench and nowhere else is his own rule and not the ward's, and he keeps it on the nights it is not needed on the grounds that a rule kept only when it is needed is not a rule.

Marmalade was a bully as a kitten and was walked home by Biff more than once. Then somebody put him in front of a bowl of dough. He bakes at night and hands it out in the morning, kittens first and usually before it is paid for, and the borough treats the bakery as the reason that stopped.

The borough side trains at five and plays on a Saturday. Teresa coaches it at a volume the allotments can hear and almost everything she bellows is praise; Sota assists without ever raising their voice and moves two paces up the line with the whole back four following; Squirt has played left wing for twenty years and does exactly what both of them say. The appeal against the county's ruling on the ferry-day postponement ran to nine pages and was won on the second.
